claims.text: Combined high-sensitivity modulated DSC and simultaneous dilatometry can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across high-entropy alloys.
Al0.5CoCrFeNi is an example of a representative single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy suitable for the proposed measurements.
HEA heat capacity can be measured by DSC from room temperature to the solidus at temperatures as high as approximately 1600 °C.
Heating and cooling through temperatures above the solidus while performing concurrent MDSC and dilatometry is a suitable measurement protocol.
Modulated temperature profiles separate reversing heat-capacity signals from non-reversing latent-heat signals during HEA melting.
High-temperature DSC measurements on HEAs can be conducted under a high-purity argon gas flow with calibrated temperature and enthalpy response.
An ultra-high-purity inert atmosphere or high vacuum prevents oxidation during the proposed high-temperature measurements.
Optimizing heating and cooling rates and modulation frequencies will resolve overlapping thermal events in multicomponent alloys.
The combined heat-flow and strain signals capture melting onset, latent heat, and the associated volume change.
Modulated DSC stabilizes the baseline and isolates the melting latent-heat event from reversible heat capacity.
Simultaneous dilatometry tracks the dimensional expansion associated with melting and correlates it directly with the thermodynamic transition.
The dual measurement strategy yields accurate fusion parameters despite HEA compositional complexity.
Melting temperatures will be determined with an uncertainty of ±2–3%.
Fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, and melting volume change will be determined with less than 5% error.
The method will permit rapid and efficient screening across a wide range of single-phase HEAs.
DSC temperature and enthalpy measurements can be calibrated using reference calibration materials under specified measurement conditions.
The approach is primarily applicable to single-phase HEAs that remain stable during high-temperature testing.
Oxidation-prone alloys and alloys exhibiting non-equilibrium phase behavior may require adaptation of the method.
High-temperature baseline drift, oxidation, and overlapping thermal events are potential sources of measurement uncertainty.
Fusion entropy can be derived from measured fusion enthalpy and melting temperature.
